findings.claim: "No. 4 oil phase-out deadline is January 1, 2030" (stated in the Local Law 43 subIndicator, in the policyAnchors entry, and repeated as actionable advice: "the Local Law 43 deadline is January 1, 2030")
findings.whatIFound: The January 1, 2030 deadline was superseded three years ago. NYC Council passed Intro 470-A on February 16, 2023 (enacted as Local Law 32 of 2023), which prohibits No. 4 fuel oil in City-owned buildings as of July 1, 2025 and in all other buildings as of July 1, 2027. The Council press release states the deadlines verbatim: city-owned buildings July 1, 2025; all other boilers July 1, 2027, and quotes Council Member Gennaro that No. 4 oil adds ~120,000 lb/yr of fine particulate matter and that the law will prevent an estimated 16 premature deaths/yr. DOB stopped issuing and renewing permits for No. 4 boilers as of June 30, 2024. The dossier's own cited source URL (retrofitaccelerator.cityofnewyork.us/resources/heating-oil-conversions) is dead — curl returns 'Recv failure: Connection reset by peer' and WebFetch returns HTTP 503 — so the 2030 date was carried on an unfetchable source, as the dossier itself half-admitted.
findings.correction: No. 4 fuel oil is banned in City-owned buildings from July 1, 2025 and in all other buildings from July 1, 2027 under Local Law 32 of 2023 (Intro 470-A, passed February 16, 2023); DOB stopped issuing/renewing No. 4 boiler permits June 30, 2024. Approximately 3,200 buildings were still using No. 4 oil per DEP data. The action item must tell owners the deadline is July 1, 2027, not 2030.

findings.claim: "~6.65 µg/m³ citywide (author-computed unweighted mean across all 59 community districts)" with geographicScale note "DOHMH does not appear to publish one single 'citywide' PM2.5 headline number in its public materials"
findings.whatIFound: DOHMH publishes citywide PM2.5 directly, in at least three places, so ruling R3 forbids the author-computed aggregate as the headline. (1) The Environment & Health Data Portal indicator 'Fine particles (PM 2.5)' (IndicatorID 2023, MeasureID 1425, 'Annual mean') is published at Citywide, Borough, CD, UHF34 and UHF42 geographies. Citywide annual mean: 6.2551 µg/m³ (2024), 6.6593 (2023), 5.763 (2022), 10.43 (2009). Data file: raw.githubusercontent.com/nychealth/EHDP-data/production/indicators/data/2023.json, with metadata declaring AvailableGeoTypes ['Borough','CD','Citywide','UHF34','UHF42']. (2) The NYCCAS 2008-2024 report's own trend chart data (embed/pollutant-trends-data.csv on the report page) gives a citywide monitoring-site annual average of 7.492 µg/m³ for 2024 and 11.401 for 2009. (3) EH Data Portal indicator 2449 'Regulatory PM2.5 monitoring' gives a citywide regulatory-monitor annual average of 8.3 µg/m³ (2024), 10.8 (2023). I independently reproduced the dossier's arithmetic — the unweighted 59-district mean is exactly 6.6508 — so the computation is correct, but it is ~6% below DOHMH's published citywide figure and it is not the statistic DOHMH reports.
findings.correction: Headline: 6.26 µg/m³ citywide annual mean, 2024 (DOHMH Environment & Health Data Portal, NYCCAS-derived). Carry the NYCCAS monitoring-site average (7.49, 2024) and the regulatory-monitor average (8.3, 2024) as explicitly labelled subIndicators; drop the author-computed unweighted mean entirely.

findings.claim: All five borough values: "6.51 µg/m³ (author-computed unweighted mean of the Bronx's 12 community districts)", Brooklyn 6.51, Manhattan 7.84, Queens 6.07, Staten Island 6.00
findings.whatIFound: These are derived aggregates, not inventions — I reproduced all five exactly from Appendix 3 Table A3-1 (Bronx 6.508, Brooklyn 6.511, Manhattan 7.842, Queens 6.071, Staten Island 6.000). But DOHMH publishes borough-level PM2.5 annual means directly (EH Data Portal indicator 2023, MeasureID 1425, GeoType 'Borough', GeoIDs 1-5): 2024 values are Bronx 6.3941, Brooklyn 6.4444, Manhattan 7.7127, Queens 5.9450, Staten Island 5.9471. R3 requires the published figure. The ranking is unchanged (Manhattan highest, Queens/Staten Island lowest), so the substantive story survives, but the unweighted means overstate every borough by 1-2% and, as the review brief anticipated, weight Midtown (10.5) equally with Rockaway (5.3) across boroughs holding 3 to 18 districts.
findings.correction: Bronx 6.39, Brooklyn 6.44, Manhattan 7.71, Queens 5.95, Staten Island 5.95 µg/m³ (2024, DOHMH EH Data Portal, borough geography). Confidence can rise to high because these are published, not derived.

findings.claim: "Congestion pricing (since Jan 2025) is independently measured to be reducing PM2.5 in and near the Manhattan CBD" (local context), and the action item citing "DOHMH/Cornell-measured PM2.5 reductions"
findings.whatIFound: The Cornell numbers themselves are exactly right — I confirmed every figure against the Crossref record for doi:10.1038/s44407-025-00037-2, 'A first look into congestion pricing in the United States: PM2.5 impacts after six months of New York City cordon pricing', Fraser/Park/Lu/Tayarani/Deng/Gao, npj Clean Air, 8 December 2025: −3.05 µg/m³ (SE 0.022) in the CRZ, 22% off a projected 13.8 µg/m³ counterfactual, −1.07 µg/m³ across the five boroughs, −0.70 µg/m³ CBSA, rising from 0.8 µg/m³ in Week 1 to 4.9 µg/m³ by Week 20. But these are modelled counterfactual estimates of average daily MAXIMUM PM2.5, and the official agency evaluation reaches the opposite conclusion. MTA's 'Congestion Relief Zone Tolling First Evaluation Report' (mta.info/document/195631), whose air-quality chapter was analysed by DOHMH and the Barry Commoner Center at Queens College (NYCCAS), reports: inside the CRZ, spring-2025 levels of PM2.5/NO2/BC/NO were 'similar or slightly lower... though the differences were not statistically significant' (PM2.5 8.1 → 8.2 → 7.8 µg/m³ for springs 2023/2024/2025); citywide outside the CRZ they were 'effectively the same' (5.6 → 5.6 → 5.9); at the six EJ-designated sites grouped, PM2.5 was 6.3 → 6.3 → 6.3 and the NO2 patterns 'suggest that tolling is not changing the levels of vehicle exhaust at those sites'; and regionally, Q1-2025 monitor means were 'within the range of values seen in the first quarters of 2022-2024'. DOHMH's own July 1, 2025 data story likewise says only 'steady or decreasing levels' and 'we do not have enough data to draw final conclusions', and notes that during the environmental review 'modeling did not identify air pollution as a concern'. This is precisely the hoped-for-effect-stated-as-measured failure the brief warned about.
findings.correction: Rewrite as contested: the Cornell/npj study estimates a 22% reduction in daily-maximum PM2.5 against a modelled counterfactual, while the official DOHMH/NYCCAS analysis published in MTA's first-year evaluation finds no statistically significant change inside the zone, no change at EJ sites, and regional means within the pre-toll range. Remove 'independently measured to be reducing PM2.5' from context and remove 'DOHMH/Cornell-measured' from the action item.

findings.claim: "2024 community-district range: 25.1 ppb (Midtown, Manhattan CD5, highest) to 4.8 ppb (Rockaway and Broad Channel, Queens CD14, lowest)" for NO2
findings.whatIFound: Two different pollutants were spliced into one range. I parsed Appendix 3 page by page. Table A3-2 (NO2, 59 districts) has a 2024 range of 10.0 ppb (Rockaway and Broad Channel, CD14) to 25.1 ppb (Midtown, CD5), mean 15.40. The 4.8 ppb figure is the 2024 minimum of Table A3-3, which is nitric oxide (NO), not NO2 — NO ranges 4.8 (Rockaway) to 18.1 ppb (Woodside and Sunnyside, Queens CD2).
findings.correction: NO2 2024 community-district range: 10.0 ppb (Rockaway and Broad Channel, Queens CD14) to 25.1 ppb (Midtown, Manhattan CD5). Citywide NO2 declined 41% between 2009 and 2024 per the NYCCAS report (portal citywide series: 27.33 → 17.53 ppb).

findings.claim: "Citywide PM2.5 has declined 29-36% since 2009 depending on the report vintage cited by DOHMH"
findings.whatIFound: The range collapses once you read the current report. The NYCCAS Report 2008-2024 Key Findings state, verbatim: 'Citywide, annual average levels of fine particulate matter declined by 36% between 2009 and 2024, an average of 0.3 micrograms per cubic meter per year.' The 29% figure is the previous vintage's statement for 2009-2023. Separately, DOHMH's EH Data Portal citywide series implies −40% over the same 2009-2024 window (10.43 → 6.2551) because it is a different statistic (modelled citywide surface) from the NYCCAS report's monitoring-site average (11.401 → 7.492, −34.3% endpoint-to-endpoint, which DOHMH rounds/fits to 36%). Companion 2009-2024 declines: NO2 −41%, NO −62%, SO2 −98%, black carbon −56%. Ozone has no downward trend (24.3 ppb in 2009 to 32.3 ppb in 2024, DOHMH noting 2009 was anomalously cool).
findings.correction: State one figure with basis and baseline: 'declined 36% between 2009 and 2024 (DOHMH NYCCAS Report 2008-2024), ~0.3 µg/m³ per year.' Note the portal's citywide series shows −40% over the same window because it is a different statistic.

findings.claim: "A materially smaller, ozone-driven Canadian wildfire smoke advisory recurred in mid-July 2026."
findings.whatIFound: Wrong pollutant and a substantial understatement. NYC Emergency Management's own wrap-up release (July 19, 2026) says the AQI 'peaked at 289 (Very Unhealthy) at 10 PM Thursday, July 16', identifies the pollutant category as Fine Particles, describes a five-day event from Wednesday July 15 through Sunday July 19, notes that it 'arrived alongside a heat emergency' making it 'a more difficult combination' than 2023 despite 'a less extreme peak', and records that New York State distributed 'more than 100,000 masks at transit hubs' while the City distributed masks through libraries, police precincts and fire stations. The ozone reading of 105 AQI ('Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups') in the July 14 pre-event advisory appears to be what the dossier mistook for the event's driver.
findings.correction: July 15-19, 2026: a five-day fine-particle Canadian wildfire smoke event; AQI peaked at 289 ('Very Unhealthy') at 10 p.m. on July 16, concurrent with a heat emergency; 100,000+ masks distributed by New York State at transit hubs plus City distribution at libraries, precincts and firehouses. Lower peak than June 2023 but longer and compounded by heat.

findings.claim: source: "US EPA (ozone reclassification); Port Authority of NY/NJ, Clean Ports Report Card (2023 Port Emissions Inventory)" and policyAnchor "Port Authority of NY/NJ Clean Air Strategy / Clean Ports Program" sourced to the same PDF
findings.whatIFound: The Clean Ports Report Card is not a Port Authority document. Its cover page reads 'Clean Ports Report Card, Port of New York and New Jersey, Prepared by Parents Engaging Parents New Jersey, October 2, 2025'. It is an advocacy scorecard grading the Port Authority, which it awards a total score of 33.7% and a grade of 'Healthier Harbor', and which criticises 'the lack of a goal and plan to fully build out shore power by 2035' as 'a notable and urgent gap'. The underlying figures the dossier quotes are correct and verbatim from that report: 'According to the 2023 Port of New York and New Jersey Emissions Inventory, ocean-going vessel operations comprise 53% of Port NOx emissions, 36% of PM2.5 emissions, and 97% of SO2 emissions.' I could not locate a primary PANYNJ statement of those sector shares — the Port's own 2023 Air Emissions Inventory report card (panynj.gov) publishes county-level shares instead, which I have added.
findings.correction: Attribute as: PANYNJ 2023 Port Emissions Inventory as cited in the Clean Ports Report Card (Parents Engaging Parents New Jersey, October 2, 2025), which graded the Port 33.7%. Add the primary PANYNJ 2023 Air Emissions Inventory county shares.

findings.claim: Global indicator: "Transboundary/regional pollutant transport and Port of NY/NJ ocean-going vessel emissions", level 50, led by inbound ozone-precursor transport and Canadian wildfire smoke
findings.whatIFound: Ruling R2 is violated by the headline. Upwind ozone precursors and Canadian wildfire smoke are pollution arriving in NYC — done TO the city, not by it. DOHMH quantifies exactly that inbound share on the NYCCAS page: 'Between 20% and 30% of the PM2.5 in New York City's air comes from sources in areas upwind from the city, such as coal-burning power plants in the Midwest.' That belongs in supporting context, not the global headline. Two genuinely outbound, quantified channels exist and I have sourced both. (1) Freight: PANYNJ's own 2023 Air Emissions Inventory report card gives the port's share of county emissions — Union County (Elizabeth) 17.5% of NOx and 3.5% of PM2.5, Richmond (Staten Island) 12.5% NOx, Essex (Newark) 11.2% NOx, Hudson (Bayonne) 9.9% NOx, Kings (Brooklyn) 3.5% NOx — and the only monitor in NYSDEC's tri-state design-value tables exceeding the 9.0 µg/m³ annual NAAQS is Elizabeth Lab in Union County at 9.4 µg/m³, inside the port complex. (2) Ozone export: Connecticut DEEP reports that on its ten highest ozone days, Connecticut's own sources contributed under 3 ppb while New York State sources contributed over 14 ppb, and that ~95% of Connecticut's worst observed air quality is due to non-Connecticut emissions; DEEP attributes its nonattainment 'mainly' to transport from the New York metropolitan area.
findings.correction: Rebuild the global lens around NYC's outbound footprint: consumption-driven port freight whose NOx/PM2.5 lands on New Jersey and Staten Island waterfront communities, plus NYC-metro NOx exported downwind into Connecticut. Demote inbound transport and wildfire smoke to labelled subIndicators identified as pollution NYC receives. Level 50 retained because the outbound channels are quantified.

findings.claim: "Reclassified from 'Moderate' to 'Serious' nonattainment for the 2015 ozone NAAQS (70 ppb) after the area missed its August 3, 2024 attainment deadline"; and "New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut jointly petitioned for and received the 2024 'Serious' reclassification"
findings.whatIFound: The classification, the standard, the rule and the URL are all correct — the dossier's cited Federal Register document 2024-16244 is real, published and effective July 25, 2024, titled 'New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island, NY-NJ-CT 2015 8-Hour Ozone Nonattainment Area; Reclassification to Serious', and the states-requested framing is right. The sequencing is wrong. The rule text shows this was a VOLUNTARY reclassification under CAA section 181(b)(3): NJDEP requested it May 23, 2024, NYSDEC June 5, 2024, CT DEEP shortly after, and the rule took effect July 25, 2024 — BEFORE the August 3, 2024 Moderate attainment deadline, not after the area 'missed' it. EPA states 'the plain language of section 181(b)(3) mandates that we approve such a request'. The rule also sets a new attainment deadline the dossier omits: 'no later than nine years from the date of the initial designation as nonattainment, i.e., August 3, 2027'. EPA's Green Book (current as of June 30, 2026) confirms all five NYC counties remain classified Serious.
findings.correction: Reclassified Moderate → Serious effective July 25, 2024 by EPA's mandatory approval of voluntary reclassification requests from NJ (May 23, 2024), NY (June 5, 2024) and CT under CAA §181(b)(3), submitted ahead of the August 3, 2024 Moderate attainment deadline the area could not meet. New attainment deadline: August 3, 2027. Still Serious as of the Green Book dated June 30, 2026.

findings.claim: "~2,000 excess deaths per year ... about 1 in every 25 deaths citywide", year 2025
findings.whatIFound: Verbatim from the cited DOHMH press release: 'Long-term exposure to PM2.5 contributes to an estimated 2,000 excess deaths from lung and heart disease each year in NYC (1 out of every 25 deaths in NYC)'. Credit to the dossier. Two additions improve it: DOHMH's own portal indicator 'Deaths due to PM2.5' (IndicatorID 2108) gives a modelled 1,798 deaths/yr age 30+ at a rate of 33 per 100,000 for 2017-2019, down from 3,175/yr in 2005-2007, with borough numbers (Brooklyn 561, Queens 418, Manhattan 365, Bronx 320, Staten Island 134) and the highest rates in Staten Island (43) and the Bronx (37) per 100,000. Indicator 2117 gives 1,125 PM2.5-attributable pediatric asthma ED visits/yr (2017-2019). The '2,000' is DOHMH's rounded public-facing figure, not a 2025 measurement — the year field should not be 2025.
findings.correction: Keep the 2,000 / 1-in-25 figure attributed to the DOHMH press release, and add the portal's 1,798 deaths/yr (age 30+, 2017-2019) and 1,125 pediatric asthma ED visits/yr (2017-2019) with vintages stated. Year field: 2019 (data) rather than 2025 (publication).

findings.claim: "An older but more geographically complete DOHMH dataset (2016)... The full five-borough table used here... is from 2016" — presented as the only complete borough breakdown available
findings.whatIFound: Current five-borough data exists and is published. EH Data Portal indicator 2379, 'Asthma emergency department visits (age 5 to 17)', MeasureID 1196, is published at Citywide, Borough, UHF42 and CD for years through 2023: citywide 143.7 per 10,000; Bronx 239.8; Manhattan 169.1; Brooklyn 125.4; Queens 103.7; Staten Island 55.9 — a 4.3x Bronx-to-Staten-Island gap. At community-district level for 2023 the extremes are Brownsville (Brooklyn CD16) 441.8, Central Harlem 396.7 and East Harlem 375.5 against Tottenville and Great Kills (Staten Island CD3) 20.6 and Borough Park 20.7 — roughly a 21x gradient, so the dossier's '20x' disparity claim survives on current data and does not need the 2016 table. The dossier's Hunts Point-Mott Haven 266.2 (2023, UHF geography) is confirmed exactly; its 2016 UHF figures of 502.7 and 578.4 are close to the portal's revised 498.6 and 579.6.
findings.correction: Replace the 2016 five-borough table with the 2023 borough series (143.7 citywide; Bronx 239.8, Manhattan 169.1, Brooklyn 125.4, Queens 103.7, Staten Island 55.9) and the 2023 CD extremes (Brownsville 441.8 vs Tottenville–Great Kills 20.6). Retain 2016 only as a trend comparator.

findings.claim: "US EPA NAAQS, revised Feb 7, 2024 from 12 to 9.0 µg/m³ annual (NYC attains this)"
findings.whatIFound: February 7, 2024 is the signature/announcement date; the final rule 'Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter' was published in the Federal Register on March 6, 2024 and became effective May 6, 2024 (confirmed by EPA's own December 19, 2024 correction notice, which recites those dates). On attainment: NYSDEC recommended all New York areas be designated attainment for the 2024 standard, and its 2023 design values (2021-2023) for NYC monitors are all below 9.0 — Bronx IS 52 7.9, Bronx Pfizer Lab 7.7, Kings JHS 126 8.0, Manhattan IS 45 7.8, Queens College 8.1, Queens near-road 7.9, Richmond Post Office 8.3. EPA's Green Book (June 30, 2026) shows no NYC county designated nonattainment for any PM2.5 standard (1997 and 2006 standards: maintenance since April 18, 2014). But EPA's designations page for the 2024 standard was still marked 'will continue to be updated' as of December 29, 2025, and Earthjustice filed a notice of intent to sue over the missed designations deadline on February 10, 2026, so 'NYC attains this' should be phrased as 'not designated nonattainment; monitor design values are below 9.0' rather than as a completed formal finding. Also worth flagging: DOHMH's citywide regulatory-monitor annual average was 10.8 µg/m³ in the 2023 wildfire year, above the standard.
findings.correction: 'US EPA annual PM2.5 NAAQS lowered from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³ (rule signed February 7, 2024, published March 6, 2024, effective May 6, 2024). No NYC county is designated nonattainment for any PM2.5 NAAQS; 2021-2023 design values at NYC monitors run 7.7-8.3 µg/m³.'

findings.claim: policyAnchor Local Law 97: "DOB began issuing the first Notices of Violation and penalties ($268/ton CO2e over the cap) around May 1, 2026"
findings.whatIFound: The cited page (now at accelerator.nyc/building-laws/ll97, redirected from accelerator.nyc/ll97) confirms the $268/ton penalty, the 2024-2029 first compliance period, 'less than 10% of properties exceeded their cap for the first 2024-29 compliance period' and 'approximately 57% are projected to exceed limits for the 2030-2034 period'. It does not mention Notices of Violation issued around May 1, 2026; the 2026 dates it gives are a June 30, 2026 filing-extension application deadline and an August 29, 2026 extended filing deadline. The NOV claim is unsourced.
findings.correction: Drop the specific May 1, 2026 NOV claim or mark it unverified; keep the verified penalty rate, compliance period, and the <10% / ~57% figures.

findings.claim: "NYC's AQI peaked around 465 on June 7, 2023 (figures reported across sources range roughly 350-465...)"
findings.whatIFound: NYC Emergency Management's July 14, 2026 advisory states: 'New Yorkers will recall the June 2023 event, when wildfire smoke drove New York City's AQI to hazardous levels, peaking at 465.' Independent accounts put the intraday peak higher — the Royal Meteorological Society and CREA report the AQI reaching 484 by 5 p.m. on June 7, 2023 with a record daily-average PM2.5 of 117 µg/m³. The dossier's stated range is honest; the upper bound should be 484 rather than 465.
findings.correction: Widen the reported range to 'roughly 465 (City figure) to 484 (5 p.m. peak reported by RMetS/CREA), with a record daily-average PM2.5 of 117 µg/m³'.

findings.claim: Local Law 43 subIndicator: "100% of NYC buildings converted off No. 6 oil by the June 30, 2015 deadline (over 6,000 heating-system conversions, >75% to the cleanest fuel options)... Buildings burning No. 4/No. 6 oil were only ~1% of buildings but were responsible for an estimated 86% of citywide soot (PM2.5) from heating"
findings.whatIFound: The cited source URL is dead (connection reset / HTTP 503), so nothing on this page is verifiable as cited. The June 30, 2015 No. 6 deadline and the 86%-of-soot framing are widely and consistently reported in secondary sources — the '1% of buildings / 86% of soot' claim traces to NYC Clean Heat and PlaNYC-era materials, and EDF's heating-oil work identified ~9,000 buildings burning residual oil — but I could not confirm the '6,000 conversions' or '>75% to cleanest fuel options' figures from any live primary source. Local Law 43 of 2010 itself is real and correctly numbered: signed by Mayor Bloomberg on August 16, 2010, requiring conversion off No. 6 by 2015. DOHMH independently corroborates the outcome: 'SO2 levels have gone down dramatically since Local Law 43 of 2010 prohibited the burning of heavy fuel oil (No. 6)', with SO2 down 98% since 2009 and now comparable to Whiteface Mountain in the Adirondacks.
findings.correction: Keep the LL43 identification, the June 30, 2015 No. 6 deadline, and DOHMH's SO2 evidence (−98% since 2009, now comparable to Whiteface Mountain). Drop the unsourceable 6,000-conversions and >75% figures; retain the 1%-of-buildings/86%-of-soot framing labelled as a PlaNYC-era NYC Clean Heat estimate. Replace the dead URL.

findings.claim: Ozone subIndicator: "2024 community-district range: 27.1 ppb (Midtown... lowest) to 38.4 ppb (Rockaway and Broad Channel... highest)"
findings.whatIFound: Confirmed exactly from Appendix 3 Table A3-5: 2024 summertime-average ozone ranges from 27.1 ppb (Midtown, CD5) to 38.4 ppb (Rockaway and Broad Channel, CD14), 59-district mean 33.3 ppb. The NOx-titration explanation matches DOHMH's own text ('In areas with heavy traffic, NOx reacts with any ground-level O3 to reduce O3 concentrations'). Worth adding the trend DOHMH reports: citywide summertime ozone has varied 27.8-33.7 ppb between 2010 and 2024 with no consistent trend, was 32.3 ppb in 2024, and DOHMH expects it to trend higher with warming.

levelReview.reasoning: The headline alone supports something close to 25: DOHMH's published citywide annual mean of 6.26 µg/m³ (2024) is 25% above the WHO 2021 guideline of 5 µg/m³, no NYC county is designated nonattainment for PM2.5, monitor design values run 7.7-8.3 against a 9.0 NAAQS, and the trend is strongly favourable (PM2.5 −36%, NO2 −41%, black carbon −56%, SO2 −98% since 2009). Per R1 the level must then be adjusted for well-sourced shortfalls inside the same dimension, and there are four material ones. (1) Ozone: all five boroughs sit in 'Serious' 2015-ozone-NAAQS nonattainment with an August 3, 2027 attainment deadline, and NYCCAS shows no downward ozone trend at all (24.3 ppb in 2009 to 32.3 ppb in 2024) with DOHMH expecting it to worsen with warming — a dimension cannot be 'mild' when the region formally fails a health standard and the failing pollutant is flat-to-rising. (2) Mortality and morbidity burden: DOHMH attributes ~2,000 excess deaths/yr (1 in 25 deaths citywide) to long-term PM2.5, with a modelled 1,798 deaths/yr age 30+ and 1,125 pediatric asthma ED visits/yr in the 2017-2019 vintage. (3) Distributional failure: child asthma ED visits range from 441.8 per 10,000 in Brownsville to 20.6 in Tottenville–Great Kills (2023), roughly 21x, and Manhattan's PM2.5 (7.71) is 30% above Queens's (5.95) with Midtown at 10.5 — the citywide mean conceals an exposure gradient the dimension exists to show. (4) Episodic overshoot: two severe wildfire-smoke events in three years (AQI 465 in June 2023, AQI 289 across five days in July 2026 alongside a heat emergency), and the 2023 citywide regulatory-monitor annual average of 10.8 µg/m³ exceeded the federal standard outright. On the other side, R5 forbids manufacturing a crisis: this is a city with a genuine multi-decade improvement record, the most granular urban monitoring network in the US, and a documented policy win in the residual-oil phase-out. 100 would be doom inflation and 25 launders the ozone failure and the mortality burden. 50 — 'needs attention' — is the honest reading. The global lens stays at 50: the outbound channels are now quantified (port share of county NOx up to 17.5%, the only tri-state monitor above the 9.0 NAAQS sitting inside the port complex at 9.4 µg/m³, and NY-source contributions above 14 ppb on Connecticut's worst ozone days), so R2's requirement for quantification is met and a score rather than null is justified.

sourcesIndependentlyFetched.confirms: NYCCAS Report 2008-2024 Key Findings: PM2.5 −36%, NO2 −41%, NO −62%, SO2 −98% between 2009 and 2024; PM2.5 −0.3 µg/m³/yr; 2024 seasonal site range 1.6-28 µg/m³; ozone no consistent trend, citywide summer average 27.8-33.7 ppb 2010-2024; 20-30% of NYC PM2.5 from upwind sources; 73 routine + 11 EJ monitoring sites in 2024; Local Law 43 of 2010 credited for the SO2 collapse
DOHMH's underlying citywide annual-average series: PM2.5 11.401 (2009) → 7.492 (2024), with 8.706 in the 2023 wildfire year; NO2 27.33 → 17.53 ppb; summertime O3 24.31 → 32.31 ppb; BC 1.253 → 0.606

All six community-district tables parsed. PM2.5 2024: 59 districts, min 5.3 (Rockaway CD14), max 10.5 (Midtown CD5), unweighted mean 6.6508 — reproducing the dossier's arithmetic exactly, including all five borough means. NO2 2024 range 10.0-25.1 ppb (refuting the 4.8 figure, which is NO). Summertime O3 2024 range 27.1-38.4 ppb

The EH Data Portal's indicator metadata declares 'Fine particles (PM 2.5)' Annual mean at AvailableGeoTypes ['Borough','CD','Citywide','UHF34','UHF42'] — i.e. DOHMH does publish citywide and borough PM2.5, contradicting the dossier's dataGap
Published PM2.5 annual means, 2024: Citywide 6.2551; Bronx 6.3941, Brooklyn 6.4444, Manhattan 7.7127, Queens 5.9450, Staten Island 5.9471. Citywide 2009 10.43 (−40.0% to 2024)
Regulatory PM2.5 citywide annual average: 8.3 µg/m³ (2024), 10.8 (2023), 8.9 (2022), 9.0 (2021)

Deaths due to PM2.5, age 30+: 1,798/yr citywide and 33 per 100,000 (2017-2019), down from 3,175/yr (2005-2007); borough numbers Brooklyn 561, Queens 418, Manhattan 365, Bronx 320, Staten Island 134; highest rates Staten Island 43 and Bronx 37
PM2.5-attributable asthma ED visits under age 18: 1,125/yr citywide (2017-2019), rate 62 per 100,000

Child (5-17) asthma ED visit rates per 10,000, 2023: citywide 143.7; Bronx 239.8, Manhattan 169.1, Brooklyn 125.4, Queens 103.7, Staten Island 55.9. CD extremes: Brownsville 441.8, Central Harlem 396.7, East Harlem 375.5 vs Tottenville–Great Kills 20.6. UHF Hunts Point–Mott Haven 266.2 (2023), 498.6 (2016)

questionsForOrchestrator: DOHMH publishes three different citywide PM2.5 annual averages for 2024 and they disagree by a third: 6.26 µg/m³ (Environment & Health Data Portal indicator 2023, the modelled citywide surface, consistent with the borough and community-district geographies), 7.49 µg/m³ (the NYCCAS report's own average across monitoring sites, which is what the report's '36% since 2009' headline is computed on), and 8.3 µg/m³ (regulatory DEC/EPA monitors, indicator 2449, the basis on which NAAQS attainment is actually judged). I headlined 6.26 for internal consistency with the borough and district data and carried the other two as labelled subIndicators. If the portrait would rather score against the standard-comparable regulatory figure, the headline becomes 8.3 — 66% above the WHO guideline instead of 25% — and the level should go higher than my recommended 50. This is a genuine framing choice, not a data problem, and it should be made once and applied consistently across the portrait.

The regulatory monitors and the NYCCAS modelled surface disagree about which borough is worst off. On the modelled surface Staten Island is the cleanest borough (5.95, 2024); on the 2021-2023 regulatory design values the Richmond Post Office monitor is the HIGHEST in the city at 8.3 µg/m³, and DOHMH's own PM2.5 mortality rate is highest in Staten Island (43 per 100,000, 2017-2019). Staten Island has one PM2.5 monitor. I have kept the published modelled borough figures per R3 and noted the discrepancy in context, but the Staten Island borough portrait will read as 'cleanest air, highest PM2.5 death rate' and someone should decide how that is presented.

Ozone is doing most of the work in raising this dimension's level (Serious nonattainment, no downward trend, an August 3, 2027 attainment deadline) while PM2.5 is genuinely improving. If the portrait wants the wedge to read cleanly, ozone may deserve to be its own headline indicator or its own sub-dimension rather than a pull factor inside a PM2.5-led dimension.
